title: An ordinary day
goal: Describe your daily routine from waking up to going to bed, and meet the second verb family — the one used for things you do to yourself.
bekal: describe a full day's activities in order
use מִתְ־ verbs for things you do to yourself

dialogs.title: שִׂיחָה — יוֹם בְּחַיֵּי דָּנָה
dialogs.intro: Budi asks Dana what her day is like.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: דָּנָה, אֵיךְ נִרְאֶה יוֹם רָגִיל שֶׁלָּךְ?
lines.baca: danah, eikh nir'eh yom ragil shelakh?
lines.id: Dana, what's a typical day like for you?
lines.literal: dana, how looks day ordinary of-you?

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.id: I shower, get dressed, and have coffee.

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.text: לִפְעָמִים. בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל אֵין לִי זְמַן.
lines.baca: lif'amim. bederekh klal ein li zman.
lines.id: Sometimes. Usually I don't have time.
lines.literal: sometimes. in-way general there-isn't to-me time.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: And how do you get to campus?

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.id: By bus. It takes twenty minutes.

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.text: בְּשֵׁשׁ, שֶׁבַע. אַחַר כָּךְ אֲנִי מְבַשֶּׁלֶת.
lines.baca: beshesh, sheva. akhar kakh ani mevashelet.
lines.id: Six, seven. After that I cook.
lines.literal: at-six, seven. after so I cook.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: And in the evening? Do you go out?

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.text: לֹא, אֲנִי מִתְעַיֶּפֶת. הוֹלֶכֶת לִישֹׁן בְּאַחַת עֶשְׂרֵה.
lines.baca: lo, ani mit'ayefet. holekhet lishon be'akhat esreh.
lines.id: No, I'm tired. I go to bed at eleven.
lines.literal: no, I tire-myself. go to-sleep at-eleven.

notes: **Verbs starting with מִתְ־ are the second family to get to know** (it's called הִתְפַּעֵל, *hitpa'el*). Its typical meaning: an action that **turns back on the doer**. מִתְלַבֵּשׁ = dresses oneself = gets dressed. מִתְקַלֵּחַ = showers oneself = takes a shower.

**English has a mirror for this: "-self" verbs.** *Dress yourself*, *prepare yourself*, *get yourself ready* — all actions that land back on the doer. English usually drops the "-self" (we just "get dressed"), but Hebrew builds it into the verb. Once you see this, the whole מִתְ־ group makes sense instead of being pure memorization.
**The forms are regular:** מִתְ־ + root. Masculine מִתְלַבֵּשׁ, feminine מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת, plural מִתְלַבְּשִׁים / מִתְלַבְּשׁוֹת. Exactly the ־ֶת and ־ִים pattern you mastered in unit 7.
⚠️ **מִתְקַלַּחַת, not מִתְקַלֶּשֶׁת** — the throat letter ח at the end of the root pulls the vowel toward *a*, just like שׁוֹמַעַת in unit 7. The same sound rule, back again.

**הַבַּיְתָה** ("home, homeward") uses the ending **־ָה**, meaning "toward". A leftover from ancient Hebrew, still alive in a few everyday words: הַבַּיְתָה (home), הַחוּצָה (outside), שָׁמָּה (there, thither), יָמִינָה (to the right).
**בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל** (*bederekh klal*, "usually") — literally "in the general way". A phrase that makes your story sound far more mature than just stringing verbs together.
**זֶה לוֹקֵחַ ... דַּקּוֹת** = "it takes ... minutes". Hebrew uses the verb "take", exactly like English *it takes*. One of the easy ones.

**אֲרוּחָה** = a meal: אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר (breakfast), אֲרוּחַת צָהֳרַיִם (lunch), אֲרוּחַת עֶרֶב (dinner). Notice the form אֲרוּחַת — a feminine noun changes ־ָה to ־ַת when it's paired with another noun. This linked form is covered in unit 17.

grammars.title: מִתְ־ verbs: doing it to yourself
body: A small group, but full of the activities you describe every day.
after: ⚠️ Look at **מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ**: the prefix isn't מִתְ־ but מִשְׁתַּ־. When the first root letter is ש, the ת of the prefix swaps places with it. This little sound rule shows up in a few common words: מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ (use), מִסְתַּכֵּל (look at), מִצְטַעֵר (be sorry).

grammars.title: Telling a story: time connectors
body: What turns a list of verbs into a story is these little words.
after: ⚠️ **אַחֲרֵי and לִפְנֵי are followed by a NOUN**, not a clause. To attach a full clause, add שֶׁ־: אַחֲרֵי שֶׁאֲנִי אוֹכֵל (after I eat). Compare English "after lunch" vs "after I eat".

blocks.text: ⚠️ **קָם** and **מִתְעוֹרֵר** aren't the same. מִתְעוֹרֵר = your eyes open; קָם = your body gets out of bed. Israelis distinguish them in everyday speech, and the jokes about the gap between the two work there just as they do in English.
**יָשֵׁן** means "is sleeping" (a state), while **הוֹלֵךְ לִישֹׁן** means "goes to bed" (an action). הוּא יָשֵׁן = he's asleep; הוּא הוֹלֵךְ לִישֹׁן = he's going to bed.

sections.title: Describing your day: a model to copy

blocks.text: Read this paragraph out loud, then rewrite it with your own times and activities. It's the single most useful exercise in this unit.

blocks.title: יוֹם שֶׁלִּי
items: אֲנִי מִתְעוֹרֵר בְּשֶׁבַע וָחֵצִי. קֹדֶם אֲנִי מִתְקַלֵּחַ וּמִתְלַבֵּשׁ.
אַחַר כָּךְ אֲנִי אוֹכֵל אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר וְשׁוֹתֶה קָפֶה.
בִּשְׁמוֹנֶה וָחֵצִי אֲנִי יוֹצֵא מֵהַבַּיִת וְנוֹסֵעַ בְּאוֹטוֹבּוּס לָעֲבוֹדָה.
אֲנִי עוֹבֵד מִתֵּשַׁע עַד חָמֵשׁ. בַּצָּהֳרַיִם אֲנִי אוֹכֵל עִם חֲבֵרִים.
בְּשֵׁשׁ אֲנִי חוֹזֵר הַבַּיְתָה, מְבַשֵּׁל, וְאוֹכֵל אֲרוּחַת עֶרֶב.
בָּעֶרֶב אֲנִי קוֹרֵא אוֹ רוֹאֶה טֶלֶוִיזְיָה, וּבַסּוֹף הוֹלֵךְ לִישֹׁן בְּאַחַת עֶשְׂרֵה.

blocks.text: Notice that the whole story uses the **present tense** — Hebrew describes habits with exactly the same form as "is doing". These six sentences are enough to answer "tell me about your day" fluently.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right time connector.
items: ____ אֲנִי מִתְקַלֵּחַ, אַחַר כָּךְ אֲנִי אוֹכֵל. (first)
I go to bed at eleven at night.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: הִיא מִתְעוֹרֶרֶת בְּשֵׁשׁ. — הִיא מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת מַהֵר. — הִיא חוֹזֶרֶת הַבַּיְתָה. — הִיא מְבַשֶּׁלֶת אֲרוּחַת עֶרֶב. — הִיא מִתְקַשֶּׁרֶת לְאִמָּא.
קֹדֶם — לִפְנֵי — אַחֲרֵי — כָּל יוֹם — בַּסּוֹף

אֲנִי מִתְעוֹרֵר בְּשֵׁשׁ וָחֵצִי. — הִיא חוֹזֶרֶת בְּשֵׁשׁ. — בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל אֲנִי לֹא אוֹכֵל אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר. — אַחֲרֵי הָעֲבוֹדָה אֲנִי מְבַשֵּׁל. — אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ לִישֹׁן בְּאַחַת עֶשְׂרֵה בַּלַּיְלָה.
הִיא מִתְעוֹרֶרֶת בְּשֶׁבַע — אֲנִי נוֹסֵעַ בְּאוֹטוֹבּוּס לָעֲבוֹדָה — בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל אֵין לִי זְמַן — בַּסּוֹף אֲנַחְנוּ הוֹלְכִים לִישֹׁן
wave: Write six sentences about your own day, following the יוֹם שֶׁלִּי model in this unit. Keep what you write — you'll rewrite it in the past tense in unit 15.
